name: Design a Global DNS Service
intent: Run the authoritative side of DNS for millions of customer domains: answer billions of queries a day in milliseconds from anywhere, change records within seconds, steer traffic away from failures, and stay up under attack.
codeTitle: zone answers, failover policy, TTL and rate limiting
finalIntro: A customer's server fails, and a user's resolver learns about it.
prompt: Design a DNS hosting service like Route 53 or Cloudflare DNS. Customers create zones and records through an API. The world's resolvers (the servers that look names up for users) send queries to our name servers, which must answer fast from everywhere. Support weighted, latency, geographic and failover routing driven by health checks, DNSSEC signing, and resist DDoS attacks. Customers must see a record change live within seconds, and the service must stay up even when a whole site is lost.
functional: Create, update and delete zones and records (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SOA and others) through an API
Answer queries from resolvers with the right records and a TTL (how long a resolver may keep the answer), or with NXDOMAIN (the name does not exist)
Route traffic by weight, by the user's location or latency, and by failover when a health check fails
Sign zones with DNSSEC so validating resolvers can check the answers
Support zone transfers (AXFR and IXFR) so a customer can run a second provider
nonFunctional: Answer a query in a few milliseconds from the nearest site, at millions of queries per second overall
Publish a record change to every site within a few seconds
Availability of 100% of queries is the goal: the service is a dependency of everything else
Detect a failed endpoint within about 30 seconds and stop answering with it
Survive attacks of hundreds of gigabits per second, including spoofed reflection traffic
Keep each site's footprint small: all zone data in memory, with no database call per query

firstAttempt.text: A few name server machines in one data centre run a standard DNS server. Each reads its records from a SQL database on every query, and the customer's changes are written to that database. Health checks are a cron job that edits records by hand when something fails.
limits: A database call per query cannot reach millions of queries per second, and a database outage takes DNS down with it
One site is far from most users, so every lookup pays a long round trip, and losing the site loses all of DNS
UDP queries with a spoofed source make the servers a weapon, and an attack fills the single data centre's link
Failover by a manual edit is slow, and nothing decides which of several healthy servers to return
Nothing signs the answers, so a validating resolver cannot tell real answers from forged ones

steps.title: Answer from memory at anycast name servers in many sites
steps.problem: Millions of queries per second from every continent cannot be answered by a database in one place, and a single site is both far away and a single point of failure.
steps.fix: Run name servers in dozens of sites and give every site the same IP addresses, announced by BGP, the protocol routers use to tell each other which addresses they can reach. This is anycast: the network sends each resolver's query to the nearest site, and if a site fails and withdraws its announcement, the same query lands on the next nearest one within seconds. Each name server holds every zone in memory in a compact tree keyed by the reversed domain labels, with answers prepared in wire format, so a query is a lookup and a copy with no disk and no database. DNS is mostly small UDP packets, so one modern server can answer hundreds of thousands of queries per second per machine.
steps.tradeoff: Low latency, huge capacity and automatic rerouting come almost for free. Every site needs the whole data set in memory, so the design depends on getting changes to every site, and anycast can send one resolver's TCP connection to two sites if routes shift mid-connection, which is rare because DNS over TCP is short.

steps.title: Store zones in a replicated database and push changes to every site
steps.problem: Customers change records all the time and expect to see them live in seconds, but every site holds its own copy in memory.
steps.fix: Customers call the control API, which writes the change to a replicated zone database that is the source of truth, with a version number per zone. Each change is also put on a change feed. Every site subscribes, applies the change to its in-memory copy, and acknowledges the version it has reached. A new or restarted site loads a snapshot and then catches up from the feed, so it never needs to read the database at query time. For customers who run another provider, the service also speaks zone transfers: IXFR sends only the changes since a serial number, AXFR sends the whole zone.
steps.tradeoff: Queries never touch the database, so a database outage stops edits but not answers. A change reaches the sites in seconds, not instantly, so sites briefly disagree, and resolvers that cached the old answer keep it until its TTL ends. Updates are tiny, so the push traffic is a small fraction of the query traffic.

steps.title: Add routing policies driven by health checks
steps.problem: Customers want one name to give different answers: split traffic 70 to 30, send users to the nearest region, and move away from a server that has stopped working.
steps.fix: A record can carry a policy. Weighted records pick among the healthy values in proportion to their weights, latency and geographic records choose by the resolver's network location (or the client subnet if the resolver sends it), and failover records return the primary until it is unhealthy and then the secondary. Health checkers in several regions probe each endpoint every 10 or 30 seconds and mark it unhealthy after a number of consecutive failures. The result goes onto the same change feed, so the policy tables in every site use the new health state within seconds. If every endpoint looks unhealthy, the answer fails open and returns them all, because a wrong guess is better than no answer.
steps.tradeoff: One name can steer traffic without any change on the customer's side. Detection time is the check interval times the failure threshold, plus a few seconds to publish, plus the TTL that resolvers cache the old answer for. Shorter intervals and thresholds find failures faster and also cause false alarms, and the answer depends on where the resolver is, not the user, so geographic steering is approximate.

steps.title: Sign the zones with DNSSEC
steps.problem: Plain DNS answers can be forged on the way to a resolver, and a resolver cannot tell a real answer from a fake one.
steps.fix: Each zone has a zone signing key that signs every record set, and a key signing key that signs the zone's key set; a hash of the key signing key (the DS record) is published in the parent zone, which builds a chain from the root down. The service uses modern elliptic-curve keys (ECDSA P-256) so signatures are small. Static records are signed ahead of time by a signer that holds the keys in hardware security modules, with each signature valid for about a week and renewed long before it expires. Records that depend on the query, such as policy answers, are signed online by the name server on demand using a key it holds, and the signature is cached. Non-existence is proved with compact NSEC or hashed NSEC3 records.
steps.tradeoff: Resolvers can detect forged answers. Offline signing keeps the keys safest but cannot cover answers that are computed per query, and online signing covers them at the cost of keys in every site and some CPU. Signed answers are several times larger, which makes amplification worse and pushes some of them over UDP size limits. The worst failure is operational: if signatures expire or keys are rolled badly, every validating resolver treats the whole zone as broken.

steps.title: Defend against floods and reflection attacks
steps.problem: DNS runs mostly over UDP, where the source address of a query can be forged. Attackers send small queries with the victim's address as the source, and our large signed answers go to the victim, with 20 to 50 times the volume of the query. Other attackers simply flood the name servers.
steps.fix: Anycast spreads a flood over every site, so each absorbs only the share that reaches it, and capacity is planned at many times the normal peak. A filter in front of the servers drops malformed packets and applies response rate limiting: it counts responses per client network prefix and name, answers only a few per second and replaces some of the excess with a tiny truncated reply, which makes a real client retry over TCP and gives a forged request nothing to amplify. Responses are kept small by answering ANY queries minimally and by avoiding unneeded records. Heavy queries such as random sub-name floods are rate limited by pattern, and sites under heavy attack can shed to others by changing their announcements.
steps.tradeoff: The service stays up under attack and cannot be used as a weapon. Rate limits must be set so that legitimate big resolvers, which send many queries from a few addresses, are not caught, which usually means a higher limit or an allow list for them. Attackers move to many different victims and names, so the limiter is a first defence and needs the network capacity behind it.

steps.title: Plan for resolver caches and for the loss of the provider
steps.problem: Resolvers, not users, talk to the service, and they cache answers by their own rules. The provider is also a dependency of its customers: if it is down, their domains vanish.
steps.fix: Treat the TTL as a product setting: a short TTL such as 30 seconds makes failover fast but multiplies the query load and makes more lookups slow cache misses, while a long TTL such as an hour is cheap and slow to change. Plan for resolvers that stretch short TTLs to a minimum or keep answers longer, and for negative caching: an NXDOMAIN or empty answer is cached for the SOA minimum value (a timer set in the zone), so a record created right after a failed lookup can stay invisible for that long. For provider failure, customers list name servers from two independent providers in their delegation, with the same zone kept in step by zone transfers or by an API sync, and resolvers use whichever answers. The service itself keeps a diverse set of anycast prefixes and separate networks, so one routing mistake cannot hide all name servers.
steps.tradeoff: Customers choose their own balance of failover speed against cost. Two providers survive the loss of one, but features that only one provider has, such as policy records and online signing, do not copy across, so the secondary usually serves plain records, and DNSSEC with two providers needs shared keys or a multi-signer setup.

failures.scenario: One site loses power or its network link
failures.impact: Resolvers whose nearest site was the failed one get no answers, and the share of queries that timed out is lost.
failures.answer: The name servers withdraw their route when their own health check fails, and if the whole site dies the BGP announcement disappears when its routers lose the session. Within seconds the network sends the same addresses to the next nearest site, which already has all the data in memory. Resolvers retry another of the listed name server addresses after a short timeout, so the damage is a brief pause for some users.

failures.scenario: A bad zone change is published to every site
failures.impact: A software bug or a mistaken customer action removes records or the apex of a large zone, and the change reaches the whole world in seconds.
failures.answer: Zone versions are immutable and kept, so a site can return to the previous version immediately, and the control plane rolls out risky changes to a few sites first and watches error and NXDOMAIN rates before the rest. Validation refuses a zone without an SOA or NS record set, and the customer can roll back to an earlier version. Because resolvers keep the old answers for the TTL, a quick rollback often repairs the damage before most users see it.

failures.scenario: DNSSEC signatures expire or a key roll goes wrong
failures.impact: Validating resolvers, including the big public ones, return SERVFAIL for the whole zone, and the site looks down to a large share of users even though every server is healthy.
failures.answer: Signatures are made with a validity of days and renewed when a third of it is gone, so a signer outage has to last days to matter, and monitors alert on the time left on the oldest signature in every zone. Key rolls follow a published sequence that waits for the cached TTLs before removing anything old. If it still breaks, removing the DS record from the parent turns validation off for the zone, which takes the parent's TTL to take effect.

failures.scenario: A reflection attack uses the service against a victim
failures.impact: Spoofed queries make the name servers send hundreds of gigabits of answers to the victim, and the provider's own links and reputation suffer.
failures.answer: Response rate limiting counts responses per client prefix and name, so the victim's prefix gets a handful of full answers per second and tiny truncated replies for the rest, and the traffic that leaves our network drops to about the size of the attacker's own queries. Minimal ANY responses and a modest UDP size reduce the gain further. Networks that filter spoofed source addresses at the edge are the real fix, but they are not under our control.

failures.scenario: The health checkers wrongly mark every endpoint down
failures.impact: A network problem between the checkers and the customer, or a bug in the checkers, makes healthy servers look dead, and failover would send everyone to a standby that cannot take the load or remove all answers.
failures.answer: A health check passes if enough of the checker regions agree, not only one, so a single region's bad path does not trigger anything. When all values of a record look unhealthy, the name server fails open and returns all of them, because a guess is better than an empty answer. Changes to health state are also limited in how fast they may flip, to avoid flapping.

alternatives.title: How the nearest site is chosen

options.name: Anycast for all name server addresses
options.pro: The network finds the nearest working site, and failure and attack spreading are automatic
options.con: Routes can shift mid-connection, and the best path is not always the lowest latency

options.name: Unicast addresses with geographic DNS for the name servers
options.pro: Precise control over which site answers
options.con: Needs DNS to find the DNS, and a failed site stays in use until caches expire

alternatives.pick: Anycast, with several different prefixes in different networks.

alternatives.title: Online or offline DNSSEC signing

options.name: Offline: sign ahead of time, keep keys in a vault
options.pro: Keys never sit on the servers that face the internet, and answers are served as stored
options.con: Cannot sign answers that are computed per query, such as weighted or latency policies

options.name: Online: sign each answer when it is built
options.pro: Works with any policy and with wildcard-like generated records
options.con: Keys live in every site, signing costs CPU, and a compromise of a server exposes a key

alternatives.pick: Offline for static records, and online signing with short-lived keys only for policy answers.

alternatives.title: How changes reach the sites

options.name: Push through a change feed
options.pro: Seconds of delay, and each site applies only the small difference
options.con: Needs a feed that is reliable, ordered per zone and replayable

options.name: Sites poll the database or pull zone transfers
options.pro: Simple and each site is independent
options.con: Delay is the poll interval, and a thousand sites polling add load

alternatives.pick: Push by a feed per zone version, with a periodic full comparison to repair any site that missed a change.

alternatives.title: How long the TTL should be

options.name: Short, such as 30 seconds
options.pro: Failover and changes are seen within a minute, even by well-behaved resolvers
options.con: Many times more queries, more cache misses that wait for a round trip, and no help from resolvers that stretch it

options.name: Long, such as one hour or a day
options.pro: Cheap, and resolvers answer almost every lookup from cache, even through a brief outage of the name servers
options.con: A bad record or a dead server stays in use for the whole TTL

alternatives.pick: Five minutes for ordinary records, and 30 to 60 seconds only on names that use health-checked failover.

roles.label: Resolvers and origins
roles.description: Recursive resolvers that ask the questions, and the customer's servers the answers point to.

roles.label: Name servers
roles.description: The anycast name servers, the control API and any second provider.

roles.label: Change feed
roles.description: Ordered zone and health changes on their way to every site.

roles.label: Policy and checks
roles.description: Routing policies, health checkers, the DNSSEC signer and the attack filter.

roles.label: Zone data
roles.description: The replicated zone database and each site's in-memory copy.

quiz.question: A DNS provider runs six name servers in one data centre. Each answers by running a SQL query. At peak the fleet gets 2 million queries per second, and the database can serve about 20,000. Customers also complain that users in Asia see slow lookups. What change fixes both problems?
options: Put a 60-second query cache in front of the SQL database and add read replicas in each region to absorb the cache misses
Run name servers at many sites on shared anycast addresses, each with every zone in memory, updated from a feed
Shard the zone table by domain name across 100 database servers, so that each one sees about 20,000 queries per second
Move the database to faster SSD storage and add connection pools in each name server, to cut the cost per query
quiz.explanation: Queries must not touch a database at all: each site keeps every zone in memory, so a lookup is a memory read and the nearest site answers. A cache or shards still leave a database in the query path and keep DNS in one place, and a cache also hides customer edits for its whole TTL. Faster disks and connection pools make each query cheaper but leave the database and the distance to Asia unchanged.

quiz.question: A customer uses failover routing. Health checks run every 10 seconds, an endpoint is marked unhealthy after 3 failures in a row, and the change reaches all sites in about 3 seconds. The record's TTL is 300 seconds. The customer wants resolvers to stop using a dead server within about 60 seconds in the worst case. What is the most effective change?
options: Lower the failure threshold from 3 checks to 1, so the endpoint is marked unhealthy after a single failed check
Run the health checks from more regions, so each failure is confirmed by more independent checkers than before
Add more anycast sites, so the name server answering each query is closer to the resolver that asks it
Lower the record TTL to about 20 seconds, accepting more query load, since caching is most of the delay
quiz.explanation: Worst case is check interval times threshold (30 s), plus publish (3 s), plus the TTL (300 s), about 333 s. The TTL dominates, so cutting it to 20 s gives about 53 s. A threshold of 1 saves only 20 s and adds false alarms, and more regions or sites do not shorten what resolvers have cached.

quiz.question: Attackers send small UDP queries for a signed zone with the victim's address forged as the source. Each 60-byte query brings back a 3,000-byte answer to the victim. Large public resolvers legitimately send tens of thousands of queries per second from a few addresses. How should the name servers respond?
options: Apply response rate limiting per client prefix with truncated replies, and give big known resolvers a higher limit
Accept UDP queries only when they are shorter than 100 bytes, and move every answer longer than that onto TCP connections
Set one fixed limit of 10 queries per second per source address, with no exceptions, and drop everything above that limit
Stop signing the answers of any zone that is being queried by an unusually large number of different source networks
quiz.explanation: Response rate limiting caps what a forged victim prefix receives, and the truncated reply makes a real resolver retry over TCP while giving a spoofer nothing to amplify. A flat low limit would cut off the big legitimate resolvers, and the query size is not what makes the attack work, the answer size is, so a 100-byte cap on queries stops nothing. Unsigning zones removes DNSSEC protection for every honest user and still lets the spoofed queries through.
